Write a note to a friend about lessons from rebuilding a service people depend on every day. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
Hi Sam,

You asked what I'd learned from the rebuild, so here it is, while it's still fresh.

The first lesson is that people who depend on a service every day don't want it to be better. They want it to keep working. We spent months talking about the new design, and users cared about one thing: whether the thing they did at 8am every morning still took the same two minutes. When we moved a button, we got more complaints than when we fixed a problem that had been costing them an hour a week. In short, the small habits matter more than the big features.

Second, go and watch people use it. We thought we understood the old service. We didn't. Staff had built workarounds we'd never heard of, and a couple of them were holding up whole processes. If we had switched the old system off on the plan we first drew up, we'd have broken things we didn't even know existed. Sitting beside a user for an afternoon told us more than three weeks of requirements workshops.

Third, don't try to replace everything in one go. It's tempting, because a clean cut-over looks tidy on a plan. But it puts all the risk in a single weekend and leaves no way back. We ran old and new side by side, moved a small group over first, and listened hard to what went wrong. It was slower, and I won't pretend it wasn't frustrating, but every problem we found was a small one, and that's the whole point.

Fourth, be honest early. When we told users what was changing, and what might go wrong, they were remarkably forgiving. When something broke, they'd already been warned, and a good number of them reported the fault before we'd spotted it. Trust you build in the quiet weeks is what you spend on the bad day.

Last, the team. Rebuilding something people rely on is tiring, and the pressure never really lets up. The people who coped best were the ones who could say "I don't know yet" without worrying about it. I'd put that ahead of any technical skill when you're hiring.

I'd happily go through any of this over a coffee. If you're thinking about a similar project, don't hesitate to get in touch. I'm counting on you to tell me what I've got wrong.

Best,
